title: What Shapes Fish n‐3 Long‐Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Composition? A Systematic Review of Influencing Factors
content:
ABSTRACT

Fish are important sources of n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 LC-PUFA), particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), but tissue EPA and DHA concentrations can vary widely in response to multiple interacting drivers whose relative importance remains unclear. This review systematically synthesised factors affecting fish muscle n-3 LC-PUFA composition. Across 3780 records from 1685 articles, the evidence base was highly uneven: dietary drivers were repeatedly tested across species, whereas most environmental and management factors had sparse, species-specific replication. Article-level directional scoring revealed a consistent core pattern: muscle EPA and DHA primarily reflected dietary n-3 LC-PUFA supply. Several dietary additives, including amino acids, prebiotics and antioxidants, also increased muscle EPA and DHA. Among non-dietary factors, higher salinity was more consistently associated with higher muscle EPA and DHA than temperature, whose effects varied strongly with context. Trade-offs between nutritional value and production performance were clearest under feed restriction and high stocking density. Both tended to elevate EPA and DHA while reducing growth, whereas reduced lipid deposition was observed only under feed restriction. Where pathway indicators were reported, dietary LC-PUFA supply showed negative feedback with endogenous bioconversion: higher supply was associated with lower desaturation and elongation, and vice versa. These findings identify robust cross-species drivers and key evidence gaps, providing a stronger evidence base to guide nutritional strategies, experimental research, and future efforts to predict and optimise EPA and DHA retention in aquaculture.
